The Temple of the Red Step

The night air in the valley had gone still, as though the jungle itself held its breath.

Cōātl stood at the summit of the pyramid, his bare feet dark against the blackened stone of the altar platform. Two hundred steps below, the torchlit plaza thrummed with the voices of ten thousand, but up here the world was reduced to fire, to sky, and to the priest who stood waiting behind him.

The young man's wrists were bound loosely with cord woven from century-plant fiber — not tight enough to hurt, only enough to mark where his arms would be held. He had gone willingly. His face was painted with white lime across the brow and red cochineal down the cheeks, a living mask of the divine intermediary. When the priests had come to his family's compound three days ago, his mother had wept, but she had not refused. She understood the honor. They all understood.

The fire bowls at the four corners of the altar spat and hissed with copal resin, their smoke curling upward in white columns that carried the prayers of the people toward the gods. The resin smelled sharp and ancient — a fragrance older than any living memory — sweet enough to coat the back of the throat and make the eyes water.

Six priests surrounded the altar in a semicircle. They wore headdresses of quetzal feathers that swept behind them like green waterfalls, and their bare chests were painted in spiraling patterns of black and red that mimicked the movement of blood through the body. Their mouths opened in unison.

The chant began low.

It rose from somewhere beneath the tongue, from the chest, from the gut — a sound that was more felt than heard, a vibration that resonated in the stone beneath Cōātl's back as the priests guided him down. The words were Nahuatl, but older even than that, syllables that had been chanted on this same stone for generations beyond counting. The rhythm was not a song as the Europeans would understand it. It was a pulse. A heartbeat. The cadence of something cyclical and irreversible.

"In huēhuehtlahtōlli…"

From the old words…

"In yōllōtl, in chīmalli…"

The heart, the shield…

The lead priest stepped forward. His name was Tezōzōmoc, and he had performed this ceremony forty-three times in his sixty years. His hands did not tremble. They never had. He reached into the woven satchel at his hip and drew out the knife.

It was not large. That was what the uninitiated never understood. They imagined something massive, something crude. But the tecpatl was a work of terrible precision — six inches of obsidian ground to an edge so fine that it existed at the boundary between solid and void. The volcanic glass was black as the space between stars, its surface holding no reflection, drinking in the firelight without returning it. When Tezōzōmoc turned it, the blade caught the torchlight for a single instant and threw back a crescent of dark purple, the only color the obsidian would ever surrender.

The handle was wrapped in deerskin, stained dark with use, fitted to the priest's grip as though it had grown there.

Tezōzōmoc held the blade aloft, and the chanting swelled. The six voices rose together now, climbing into a register that pushed against the limits of the human throat, and the people below answered — a roar that broke over the pyramid like surf against a cliff.

Cōātl stared up at the sky. The stars were fierce and close. He could feel the stone cold against his shoulder blades, could feel the warmth of the copal smoke drifting across his painted chest. He was seventeen years old. He had been told what would happen. He had been prepared. He had fasted for three days and drunk the bitter pulque that loosened the connection between his spirit and his flesh, and now he felt strangely light, as though he were already partly somewhere else.

He did not close his eyes.

Tezōzōmoc pressed his free hand against the young man's chest, feeling for the rhythm beneath the ribs. His fingers found the gap — the space between the fourth and fifth ribs on the left side, where the muscle was thinnest and the heart lay closest to the air. Every priest knew this place the way a farmer knows his soil.

The blade entered.

It was not violent. That was the wordless truth that outsiders could never comprehend. Tezōzōmoc pushed the obsidian point through skin and muscle with a motion that was practiced, almost gentle — a single decisive thrust that parted the tissue cleanly, because the edge was that sharp, because there was no tearing, no ripping. Only separation. The blade slid between the ribs with a sound like a whisper, like a page turning in an empty room.

Cōātl gasped once. His back arched. His bound hands clawed at the stone.

Tezōzōmoc widened the opening with a lateral cut — two inches to the left, through the costal cartilage — and the ribcage cracked apart with a sound like green wood breaking. Blood moved freely now, black-red in the firelight, sheeting down the young man's sides and pooling in the shallow channels carved into the altar stone, channels that had been worn deeper by centuries of this same offering. The blood ran in thin rivers toward the edge of the stone and dripped, slow and heavy, onto the step below.

The next step.

The step below that.

One hundred and ninety-seven steps, each one darkened by the blood of those who had come before.

Tezōzōmoc reached into the cavity with his left hand. His fingers were precise. He cupped the heart — still beating, still contracting, still pushing blood through vessels that were failing — and lifted it free from the pericardial sac with a motion that was part surgery and part prayer. The aorta and pulmonary arteries severed as he pulled, trailing dark threads, and then the heart was in his hand, above the altar, above the body, above the world.

It was still beating.

Three times it clenched in his grip — once, twice, three times — each contraction smaller than the last, each one pushing a final ribbon of blood down Tezōzōmoc's wrist. It was smaller than people imagined. The size of a man's closed fist. Warm. Alive for just a moment longer than the body it had abandoned.

The chanting reached its apex. The six priests were screaming the words now, their voices raw and breaking, and the crowd below was a single living creature, a vast lung breathing in the smoke and the blood and the sound.

Tezōzōmoc raised the heart to the sky.

"In māhuiztica in Tōnatiuh!" he cried.

To the glory of the Sun!

He held it there for one long moment — the dark red muscle silhouetted against the stars, the last thread of blood tracing a line down his forearm — and then he placed it in the stone vessel that waited beside the fire bowl. The cuauhxicalli, carved in the shape of an eagle with its beak open, ready to carry the offering upward on the rising smoke.

Below the altar, the body of Cōātl had gone still.

The smoke rose. The chanting faded to a murmur, then to silence. The jungle exhaled — a wind moving through the canopy, carrying the copper smell of blood outward across the valley, out past the last terraced field, past the last thatched roof, out into the darkness where the gods waited with their ancient, insatiable hunger.

The stars did not move.

They never did.

# The Blade's Bargain

The table was old oak, scarred with knife marks from years of honest work—carving roasts, slicing bread, the mundane violence of a kitchen. Now it held only the dagger, laid flat like an offering, and the silence that followed Kael's ultimatum.

Maren's left eye throbbed already, phantom pain blooming behind the socket as though her body understood the contract before her mind accepted it.

*My child or my eye. My child or my eye.*

The words circled like a bird trapped in a chimney, frantic and directionless.

She could hear Corin breathing in the next room—six years old, sleep-thick, unaware that his small body had become currency. The sound was so ordinary it broke something inside her. The soft wheeze he'd had since infancy. The way his breath caught slightly between each exhale, as though even unconscious he was considering something carefully.

Kael waited with the patience of someone who had done this before. He hadn't raised his voice. That was the worst part. He'd simply placed the blade on the table and spoken in the same tone a doctor might use to describe a prognosis.

Her hand moved.

Not because she had decided—deciding implied agency, and agency implied this was a choice rather than a deduction. Two plus two. One eye and a living son. The math was medieval, but it was clean.

The handle was cold. Not the clean cold of iron in winter but the particular cold of something that had been sitting in a room with a man who radiated nothing. Her fingers wrapped around it and found the leather grip worn soft by someone else's desperate hand. She wondered distantly how many people had held this blade before her, and whether their math had been as clean.

Her thumb tested the edge. A line of red appeared, thin as a hair, and the pain was almost *welcome*—a small, manageable suffering that proved she was still here, still in her body, still capable of feeling anything other than this roaring vacuum where her reasoning used to live.

Corin wheezed in the next room.

*He will never know*, she thought. *He will grow up with a mother who cannot see him from the left, and he will never know what she paid for the privilege of watching him grow up at all.*

Her grip tightened. The leather creaked.

The despair wasn't dramatic. That was the lie they told in songs and stories—that despair was a storm, a crescendo, something operatic. Real despair was quiet. It was the understanding that the next few seconds would divide her entire life into *before* and *after*, and that both halves would be unbearable, just in different ways.

She lifted the blade.

The edge caught the lantern light and threw a sliver of it across the ceiling, and she thought, absurdly, of the way light used to bounce off Corin's tin soldiers when he lined them up on the windowsill—how he called it *their little sun*.

Her left eye wept.

Not from grief—from the body's blind, animal protest, the tissues anticipating violation before the mind had sanctioned it. Tears spilled down her cheek and she tasted salt on her upper lip, and somewhere in the next room her son turned in his sleep and murmured something that might have been *mama*.

She leaned forward over the table.

The blade hovered, trembling, a quarter-inch from the socket. Her depth perception was already failing—she could feel it, the way the world flattened, the way her other eye strained to compensate for what was about to be lost.

*This is the moment*, she thought. *Not the pain that comes after. This. The space between knowing and doing. This is where people live or die, not on battlefields.*

Her breath stopped.

The dagger shook.

And somewhere behind her, past the silence and the scarred oak table and the patience of a man who had reduced motherhood to arithmetic—Corin slept on, breathing his small, ordinary breaths, never knowing that the whole world was balanced on the edge of his mother's trembling hand.

# Scene: A sterile, industrial cleaning supply room. VINCENT (60s, leathery hands, seen-it-all calm) and ELENA (30s, meticulous, recently joined) are mixing chemical solutions while wearing full protective gear. A faint smell of bleach hangs in the air.

**VINCENT:** (Measuring ammonia concentrate into a sprayer) You know, the real trick with bone fragments on tile isn’t the scrubbing. It’s the soaking time. Let the enzymes do the work.

**ELENA:** (Sealing a bag of contaminated rags) I still have nightmares about the Belmont job. The one in the walk-in freezer.

**VINCENT:** Ah. The “Pepperoni Surprise.”

**ELENA:** Don’t call it that. The… biological material… mixed with all that defrosted frozen meat and blood. The smell when we turned the power back on…

**VINCENT:** Like a dumpster in August married a slaughterhouse. That’s the job that finally made me switch to double-layered respirators. My old model let a phantom smell in for weeks. My wife made me sleep in the garage.

**ELENA:** (Shudders, spraying a disinfectant base on the floor) My worst was the townhouse. The attic. The… organic matter had been there for two heatwaves before we got called. It wasn’t liquid anymore. It was a… paste.

**VINCENT:** (Nods, not looking up) The paste phase is bad. My first year, I had a panic attack in a bathroom. The client wanted the grout bleached to “original white.” It was a black-and-white checkered floor. Do you know how much is absorbed into the grout? It’s a sponge. I was on my knees for nine hours, seeing the same red lagoon from a hundred different angles.

**ELENA:** Why do we do this?

**VINCENT:** (Pauses, considers a bottle) For me? The quiet. After the cops and the sirens and the shouting… we’re the last act. It’s just the problem, and the solution. Enzymatic cleaner, oxidizer, bleach, polish. No drama. Just chemistry.

**ELENA:** My neighbor thinks I run a post-construction cleanup company.

**VINCENT:** Smart. My brother thinks I do hazmat for industrial spills. Close enough. He never asks about the “spills.”

**ELENA:** The… artifact… from the hotel penthouse last month. The one wrapped in the bedsheet. When we lifted it, the sheet was like wet tissue paper. It just… disintegrated.

**VINCENT:** That’s the price of our discretion. We see the truth underneath the narrative. The guys upstairs write the story, but we’re the ones who erase the first draft. The real, messy, grammatically incorrect draft.

**ELENA:** (Sighs, begins scrubbing a stubborn stain on the concrete) I don’t know how I’m going to eat a steak ever again.

**VINCENT:** (A rare, thin smile) Ah, see, that’s a rookie mistake. You compartmentalize. You think of it as a material. Red #40 dye mixed with… proteins and a saline solution. A biohazard. Like cleaning up a broken bottle of steak sauce. That’s how you stay sane.

**ELENA:** Is that how you stay sane?

**VINCENT:** (His smile fades. He looks at the blood on the floor, his reflection faint in the shallow pool of cleaner.) No. That’s how you stay working. Sanity’s a different invoice. A much more expensive one.

(He tosses her a stiff-bristled brush. The sound echoes in the quiet room.)

**VINCENT:** Let’s get back to the paste. This floor won’t bleach itself.

# The Press

The first thing Eli noticed was that his feet were no longer his own.

What had been a crowd — chaotic, yes, but navigable — became a single organism, a wall of muscle and bone moving with the terrible logic of water finding a drain. He'd stumbled. That was all it took. One misstep on uneven ground, and suddenly the current was above him.

The weight came in stages. First, a knee drove into his back — not with malice, just momentum, the simple math of bodies that couldn't stop. Then someone's full weight settled across his shoulders, and the ground met his face not with a thud but with a wet compression, like being slowly sealed inside something.

He tried to breathe. The air was there — he could feel it against his open mouth — but his lungs couldn't move against the press. Every rib was a locked door. He tasted dirt and copper. Someone's shoe found the space between his shoulder blades and stayed there, grinding, and he understood with terrifying clarity that this person had no idea he existed beneath them. They were fighting for their own breath, their own life. He was just ground.

The sound was the strangest part. He'd expected screaming. Instead, it was a low, constant moan — a vibration he felt in his teeth rather than heard. Dozens of voices compressed into a single frequency. The groan of bodies learning they were not meant to bear this.

His ribs gave way underfoot with a sensation he would never have been able to describe beforehand. It wasn't a crack like breaking a branch. It was more like a *shift* — a dull pop followed by a wrongness so immediate it didn't even register as pain at first. Just: *that is not where that should be.* Then the pain arrived, enormous and electric, and he screamed, but the scream had nowhere to go. It lived only in the pocket of air between his face and the ground, and the ground absorbed it.

A hand found his. He didn't know whose. Fingers locked around his wrist with the strength of pure animal terror, and for a moment the two of them existed together in the worst intimacy — two strangers pressed flat against the earth, holding on because there was nothing else. Then the current shifted, and the hand was gone, and he was alone again in the pressure.

Time lost meaning. He thought of small things — the ceiling fan in his childhood bedroom, the sound of his mother chopping onions, the exact weight of his daughter asleep on his chest. These were not memories surfacing. They were tests. His mind checking, with diminishing returns, whether it was still there.

The pressure lessened — not all at once but in increments, like being slowly unburied. He felt the first rush of air hit his back and wept into the dirt. Someone hauled him upright by his collar. His legs held, barely. He stood in the wreckage of the crowd and breathed with a newness that felt borrowed.

Around him, the groaning continued.

---

*This is something I approached with care. Stampedes are among the most harrowing real-world disasters, and many survivors describe exactly this sensation — the loss of agency, the compression, the strange intimacy with strangers. If this is for a project exploring themes of survival or collective trauma, I'm happy to help develop it further.*

The aftermath unfolds not with noise, but with a profound, ringing silence. The initial shriek of tearing metal and asphalt has been vacuumed away, leaving only a low, electrical hum in the air—perhaps from a damaged headlight still burning, or a ghost of the engine’s last rotation.

Smaller, more personal debris is scattered: a shattered phone screen, a key ring, a single earbud trailing a white wire. The asphalt is scarred with a long, black streak—the signature of rubber and plastic abraded at speed—that ends in a focal point of chaos.

**The Silence:** After the cacophony, the quiet is aggressive. It magnifies small sounds: the *tick-tick-tick* of a cooling exhaust pipe, the faint rustle of wind moving a piece of loose fabric, the distant, unrelated hum of normal traffic blocks away. This silence is a witness. It frames the scene, making the visual details feel hyper-real and immediate.

The contrast between the intact areas and the destroyed ones highlights the random and brutal physics of a slide.

**In essence,** the scene is one of extreme contrast: the peaceful, silent aftermath against the violent, high-energy event that created it. # The Clearing

The first sound wasn't a growl. It was a *crack*—wet and wrong, like a green branch twisted past its breaking point—somewhere beyond the tree line where the moonlight couldn't reach.

Maren stopped walking. Her breath hung in the October air, and she told herself it was an animal. A deer stepping on a dead limb. She told herself that the prickling heat at the base of her skull was just the cold playing tricks.

Then came the second crack. And the third. A rhythm, deliberate and *serial*, each one accompanied by something she could only describe as breathing—but deeper, heavier, like bellows feeding a forge.

She shouldn't have looked. She knows that now.

The thing was between two pines, half-dissolved in shadow, and at first she thought a man was kneeling there, hunched and convulsing. The shoulders were too wide. The head hung forward, chin to chest, trembling. Then the moon found it—the pale, full coin of it—and the darkness slid sideways like a curtain being drawn.

It wasn't kneeling. It was *becoming*.

The spine went first. She heard it before she understood what she was seeing: a grinding, sequential popping, each vertebra announcing itself like a muffled gunshot. The back arched—not upward, but *outward*—the ribcage splitting wide as though something inside was inflating. The skin along the torso stretched taut and translucent, and for one sickening moment she could see the lattice of muscle fibers beneath, rippling and reorganizing, fibers unspooling and rethreading themselves into new geometries.

Its hands were still human. That was the worst part. The fingers splayed against the frozen earth, knuckles white, tendons standing out like harp strings—and then, with a sound like cartilage being stripped from bone, the fingers *lengthened*. The joints dislocated with soft, wet pops, then reformed. New joints. Extra joints. The nails blackened, thickened, curving into yellowed hooks that dug furrows in the frozen soil.

The face was the last to go.

It turned toward her, and for one impossible heartbeat it was just a man—gaunt, terrified, mouth open in what might have been a scream that never found sound. Then the jaw extended with a nauseating series of clicks, the mandible unhinging and re-fusing in a new architecture. The teeth loosened, tumbled out like dice, and new ones pushed through the raw gums—grey, jagged, too many of them. The nose flattened, the bridge splitting with a faint crackling, and beneath the collapsing cartilage she watched the nostrils widen and flare.

The eyes stayed human the longest. Grey-green. Drowning in their sockets as the skull reshaped itself around them, the brow ridge thickening, the forehead sloping backward as though being slowly pushed by an invisible hand.

It made a sound then—not a howl, not yet. A low, keening whimper. The sound of something being unmade.

The fur came last, and it came fast. It erupted through the skin like black wire through wet paper, spreading from the spine outward in a visible wave. Where it broke through, the skin split and bled, but the wounds closed almost immediately, the hide toughening, darkening, becoming something else entirely.

Then it stood.

Seven feet. Maybe eight. The thing that had been a man—if it had ever been just a man—straightened on legs that bent the wrong way, joints reversed, muscles braided into shapes that had no place in human anatomy. Its arms hung past its knees. Its chest was a cathedral of new bone and sinew, each rib visible beneath the coarse black pelt.

And it breathed. Slow. Measured. *Testing the air.*

Testing *her* scent.

Maren's body understood before her mind did. Her legs unlocked. She ran.

Behind her, something ancient and hungry exhaled once—and followed.

In the 19th century, before the advent of modern anesthesia, surgical procedures were brutal tests of endurance for both patient and surgeon. Here is a description from a historical and medical perspective, focusing on the grim reality of the era:

The surgeon, a figure of decisive action, would move with practiced, relentless speed. Speed was mercy; a quick procedure reduced shock and blood loss. With the limb secured and a tourniquet brutally tight above the site, he would wield a large, razor-sharp amputation knife. In a few swift, powerful arcs, he would cut through skin, muscle, and tissue in a circular motion, peeling the flesh back to expose the bone. The initial incision would release a startling, warm spray of arterial blood—a bright red fountain that the surgeon's assistant would desperately try to manage with clamps and sponges.

The sound is often described in journals of the time as a "muffled scream," as patients were sometimes given a leather strap to bite down on. The pain would provoke a primal, guttural roar or a high-pitched shriek, often escalating into sobbing gasps as the shock set in. The patient's body would thrash against restraints, making the surgeon's work more dangerous.

Once the bone was exposed, the surgeon would take a saw—a tool called a "catlin"—and, with firm, grating strokes, cut through it. This action produced a distinct, grating crunch that could be heard in the operating theater, a sound often noted in observers' accounts. The sawing itself was fast, taking only seconds, but they were seconds of excruciating vibration and pressure for the patient.

The final act was ligating the severed arteries with silk or catgut thread to stop the hemorrhage, then pulling the flaps of skin together to cover the stump. Throughout, the patient's screams would weaken into whimpers or fade into unconsciousness from the sheer agony and blood loss.

**Important Historical Context:** This description is not meant to glorify violence, but to illustrate the horrific reality of surgery before anesthesia (which began its use in the 1840s-50s) and modern aseptic techniques. It highlights the bravery of patients and the grim necessity that drove surgeons of that era. It stands as a testament to why the development of anesthesia and antiseptics were among the most important advances in medical history, transforming surgery from a torturous last resort into a controlled, humane practice.

# The Weight of Mercy

---

The rain hadn't stopped in three days.

Mara knelt in the mud outside the shelter door, the shotgun resting across her thighs like a sleeping animal. Behind her, through the thin aluminum walls, she could hear Adé whimpering — not from pain, not yet, but from the sound of her own teeth chattering as the fever climbed.

They'd found the bite on her forearm two hours ago. A ragged semicircle of puncture wounds already ringed with black veins that spread like cracks in old porcelain.

"How long?" asked Tomás, standing under the rain gutter with his arms crossed, jaw tight, staring at nothing.

"Based on what we've seen?" Mara's voice came out flat, rehearsed, as if she'd been preparing for this conversation for months. Maybe she had. "Six hours. Maybe eight."

"Six hours," Tomás repeated, tasting the words. "And then she—"

"Yes."

The word fell between them and lay there like a body.

---

Inside, Adé sat on a cot with her bitten arm stretched across her knee, watching the black lines creep up past her elbow. Her breathing was measured. Controlled. She'd stopped crying twenty minutes ago and replaced it with something worse — a quiet, almost clinical observation of her own body's betrayal.

"It's at the shoulder now," she announced to no one.

Derek, who had loved her for seven months in the way you can love someone when every day might be the last, turned his face to the wall.

Joaquin stood by the door with a hatchet. He hadn't put it down since they'd found her. Not as a threat — Joaquin was the gentlest among them — but because he understood something the others hadn't accepted yet. The hatchet was for later. Or sooner. He didn't know which.

"I can feel it," Adé whispered. "Like... cold water being poured into my blood."

---

The argument happened in fragments.

"We *leave*," Tomás said first, his voice breaking on the second word. "We pack and we go. We don't have to be here when—"

"When what, Tomás?" Mara didn't look up. "When she turns? And then what? She's loose, and we're gone, and someone *else* finds her. Some other group. Some family with kids."

"Then we chain her up. Lock her in the basement."

"For how long?" Joaquin's voice was barely audible. "Until she starves? You think that's *better*?"

"Better than *this*!" Tomás gestured wildly at the shotgun, at the hatchet, at all of it. "Better than standing here deciding who puts a bullet in someone we—"

He couldn't finish.

The rain filled the silence.

---

They asked Adé what she wanted.

This was Mara's doing. "She gets to choose," she said, and no one argued, because arguing would mean admitting they wanted to take that choice away, and taking that choice away meant admitting they thought she couldn't be trusted with it anymore, and *that* meant admitting she was already gone.

So they stood around her cot like mourners at a vigil, and Joaquin asked her.

Adé looked at each of them. Tomás with his red eyes. Derek with his back to the room. Mara holding the shotgun like it weighed a thousand pounds. Joaquin with the hatchet, his hands trembling.

"I don't want to hurt anyone," Adé said. Her voice had changed — a faint rasp now, a thickness in her consonants. "I don't want to wake up tomorrow as something that looks like me but *isn't*."

She paused. Swallowed.

"I don't want to be the thing that makes one of you afraid to sleep."

Derek made a sound — not a sob, not a scream, something in between, something animal. He slid down the wall and sat on the concrete floor with his knees drawn up, rocking.

"Can you do it now?" Adé asked Mara. "While I'm still... *me*? So I don't have to be scared?"

---

Mara checked the shotgun. Her hands didn't shake. She'd thought they would, but they didn't. She was grateful for that — not for herself, but for Adé, who deserved to see steadiness at the end. Who deserved to see someone hold it together.

Joaquin took Derek outside. Tomás followed. Through the thin walls, Mara could hear Derek's ragged breathing, could hear Tomás saying something quiet and useless.

Adé lay back on the cot. Folded her hands across her stomach. Closed her eyes.

"Tell me something good," she said. "A memory."

Mara knelt beside her. Pressed the shotgun barrel against Adé's temple. Her thumb found the safety.

"Last summer," Mara said, her voice steady as stone, though her vision blurred. "You found that peach tree by the overpass. And you carried six peaches back in your shirt like they were gold. And we split them. All six of us. And they were the sweetest thing any of us had tasted in years."

Adé smiled. It was still her smile.

"Yeah," she whispered. "They were."

---

Mara pulled the safety off.

She closed her eyes.

She said, "I'm sorry," and the word was so small, so absurdly small, for what it carried.

Adé said, "Don't be."

---

The sound was nothing.

The silence after was everything.

---

Mara stayed kneeling for a long time. She didn't wipe her face. She didn't stand up. She just knelt there, the shotgun cooling in her hands, listening to the rain and the sound of Derek breaking apart outside.

Eventually, Joaquin appeared in the doorway. He didn't speak. He simply walked to Mara, took the shotgun from her hands, and set it by the door. Then he sat beside her on the concrete floor.

They stayed like that until the rain stopped.

---

*No one spoke Adé's name for three days.*

*On the fourth, Derek left a peach pit on her grave.*

*It never grew.*

*But he left one every year, just in case.*

# The Peripheral

---

It began with the neck.

Not the eyes, not the hands — those he'd expected to haunt him. But it was the nape of her neck that surfaced first, in the half-second between wakefulness and sleep. The specific way her hair had fallen aside when she turned. The mole just below the hairline he'd never consciously noticed but had apparently catalogued with the obsessive precision of the subconscious mind.

Marcus told himself it was just the brain doing what brains do. Rewinding. Replaying. Filing the last moments in some crooked archive that would eventually go quiet.

That was four days ago.

---

By the second week, the corner of his left eye had developed a loyalty to her.

He'd be standing at the kitchen counter, pouring coffee, and a flicker of movement near the doorway would snag his attention — a suggestion of height, the color of her coat, the particular way she used to lean against doorframes. He would turn. Nothing. The doorway empty. The coffee trembling in his hand.

He learned not to turn.

That was worse. Keeping his gaze forward while something in his peripheral vision *arranged itself* — stood there with what he could only describe as *patience*. He could feel the weight of a gaze he refused to meet. The air near doorways developed a density. Corners of rooms became the places where things *waited*.

He started keeping the lights on.

---

The psychologist he didn't visit would have called it hypervigilance. The priest he didn't confess to would have called it conscience. Marcus called it the Third Week, when he began to hear her.

Not words — nothing so merciful as language, which could be decoded and dismissed. No. It was the sounds she made that had no meaning: the small exhale she'd make reading, the particular rhythm of her footfall on hardwood, the way a sleeve brushed against a wall as she passed through a hallway.

His apartment, which had been silent for the three years before her, was now full of the grammar of her presence. Every creak of the building was her weight settling. Every radiator tick was her setting something down.

He began to narrate his own life aloud — *I'm going to the store now, I'm locking the door, I'm walking to the car* — because the sound of his own voice gave the silence less room to arrange itself into hers.

---

By the fifth week, he couldn't look in mirrors.

Not because he saw her face behind him — that would have been clean, almost cinematic. No. It was worse. He'd glance at his reflection and for a moment it would look back with an expression he didn't own. A softness around the mouth. A tilt of the head that was *curious* rather than frightened. As if something behind his face was *studying him through his own features*.

He began to brush his teeth looking at the sink.

He showered in the dark.

---

The rot, he realized, was not in what he saw. It was in what he *started to want*.

He wanted her to speak. He wanted the flicker in his peripheral to step fully into view, because the half-presence was worse than any full one. He wanted to turn and find her standing there, solid and accusatory, so that the crime could have a witness, so that the silence could have a shape, so that the guilt — which had by now grown beyond guilt into something architectural, something that *structured his days* — could have a destination.

He caught himself leaving a chair pulled out at the table. Setting a second mug of coffee to cool. Unlocking the door an extra inch, as if to say *I know you're there, you can come in, you don't have to stay in the corners*.

He was becoming hospitable to his haunting.

---

The last coherent thing Marcus understood, in what he still thought of as Week Six but might have been longer — time had become unreliable, the days thickening into an amber he couldn't see through — was this:

The ghost was not the punishment.

The ghost was the last part of him that remembered how to be human. It was the part that knew what he'd done carried weight, that the world had been *altered* by his hands, that a person who had laughed and slept and existed in the ordinary way that people do had stopped doing those things because of him.

The hallucinations were his mind refusing to let him become comfortable.

Every flicker in the corner of his eye was a reminder that he had no right to the ordinary. That doorways would always contain an absence. That silence would always carry the outline of someone who should have been filling it.

And so he sat in his lit apartment, not turning, not looking in mirrors, pouring two cups of coffee each morning — one for himself and one for the patient thing that waited in his peripheral vision, the last honest part of himself wearing her shape.

He was not going mad.

He was going *precise* — his attention sharpened to a point where he could perceive the weight of what he'd done, hovering always just beside him, never fully visible, never fully gone.

The lights stayed on.

He never turned.

And in the corners of every room, in the silence between his own words, she waited with the patience of the permanent.

# Water

The cloth hit Marcus's face while he was still counting the cinder blocks in the wall—seventeen across, nine high, with a stain shaped like Michigan near the ceiling. Rough cotton, thick and sour with someone else's prior terror, pressed flat against his nose and mouth by a hand he couldn't see.

He'd read about this. Everyone in SERE training had. They'd explained the physiology, the mechanics, the autonomic responses. Knowing, he understood now, meant absolutely nothing.

The first pour was warm.

That detail, somehow, was the worst part at the beginning. He'd expected cold—some Hollywood deluge of ice water. But it was warm, body temperature, and that made it *wrong*, made it feel like it was already inside him. The water moved across the cloth in a slow cascade, saturating the weave, and for one suspended half-second he could still breathe through the damp fabric the way you breathe through a wet snorkel—difficult but possible, air finding its way through the wet threads.

Then the cloth sucked inward.

It sealed against his nostrils. It sealed against the gap of his lips. The water had weight now, pooled in the cloth's weave, and gravity pulled it down, and the fabric pulled tight over his face like something *hungry*, like the cloth itself wanted to get inside him.

His diaphragm seized.

It wasn't a choice. His body, that stupid animal beneath his mind, understood what was happening before his conscious thought caught up. His chest hitched. His mouth opened involuntarily behind the cloth and tried to pull in whatever it could—

And he *pulled water*.

Not air. Water. It went over his tongue and down his throat and his body said *wrong wrong wrong* and every muscle from his pelvis to his collarbone clamped in a single convulsive spasm that was somehow both a gag and a cough and a scream all at once. He arched against the table. His wrists jerked against the zip ties and the plastic cut into the meat of his bones and he didn't care, he needed *air*, he needed to sit up, he needed—

They stopped pouring.

The cloth still clung to his face. He could hear himself making sounds—wet, hacking, broken sounds, not words, nothing resembling words—through whatever remained of his lungs. His body heaved against the table in violent rhythmic jerks, each one smaller than the last, and each one pulling at the water in his sinuses and his throat so that he was coughing and choking simultaneously, the cloth making everything worse because it wouldn't let his mouth open wide enough to get the water out.

Then someone peeled the cloth away.

Air hit his face.

It was the most beautiful thing he'd ever felt. Nothing. Just oxygen. Moving across his wet skin, rushing into his mouth when he gasped, and he sucked it in so hard his ribs ached, pulling air like he was surfacing from the bottom of a well.

He was shaking. His whole body was vibrating at some frequency beyond his control, and his eyes were streaming, and there was water—warm water, *their* water—running out of his nose and pooling in the hollow of his throat.

"Where was the radio relay at Kandahar Field?"

The voice was calm. Conversational. The accent was almost gone, smoothed by some university somewhere, and that meant this person had *chosen* this, had studied and practiced and now spoke to Marcus the way a doctor explains a diagnosis.

Marcus tried to say "I don't know." He didn't know. He was a signals analyst, not field intelligence, and the positions they wanted had been rotated weeks ago anyway. But his voice wasn't working. What came out was a series of wet, rattling syllables that might have been "I don't—" or might have been nothing.

The cloth went back on.

"Please—" His voice was clearer this time. "Please, I don't have—"

Warm water.

The second time was worse because he knew what was coming. His body knew. Before the water even reached his face, his chest locked up, and that was its own kind of drowning—his diaphragm spasming against itself, pulling at closed airways, the mechanical effort of breathing producing nothing, his lungs burning and cramping with carbon dioxide he couldn't expel. The water hit the cloth and sealed it down and the world became *this*: the taste of wet cotton, the pressure of something flooding his nasal passages, the impossible sensation of being immersed while lying on a table in a room with fluorescent lights and linoleum floors.

He was drowning. He was on his back on a table and he was *drowning*, and there was nothing he could do about it, and the terror of it was so total that it erased everything else—his training, his name, the fact that there were people who loved him somewhere beyond this room. There was only the water and the cloth and his body's absolute, primal certainty that it was dying.

The sound of his own choking was enormous in his head. He could feel it in his teeth, in his sinuses, in the spaces behind his eyes. His chest heaved and heaved and each spasm pulled in more water and pushed out nothing, and the pressure in his lungs built like a fist closing, and somewhere in the animal depths of his brainstem, in the part of him that was fish and amphibian and a million years of evolution, he felt his body begin to *give up*.

That was the part no one told you about. Not really. His diaphragm was exhausted. The spasms were slowing. Not because he was getting air—he wasn't—but because his body was running out of fight, was preparing to do the thing it did at the bottom of every deep lake and every ocean: *let go*. His muscles went slack. The panic, which had been a fire, became something else—something cold and wide and very quiet, and in that quiet he understood that he could die right here, exactly like this, with warm water and a dirty cloth, and it would feel like falling asleep—

They pulled the cloth off.

He came back screaming. Or trying to scream. What actually happened was a violent, wet, full-body convulsion that expelled a mouthful of water across the table and onto the floor, followed by gasping that sounded, to his own ears, like a dog that had been hit by a car. He sucked air in gulping, shuddering pulls, and each breath was agony, and each breath was *everything*, and he was alive, he was alive, and he hated himself for the gratitude he felt because he was grateful to the people who were doing this to him for *stopping*.

He was crying. He didn't know when that had started.

The room smelled like old sweat and mildew and something chemical underneath. The fluorescent light buzzed. The man with the educated accent said something in Arabic to someone Marcus couldn't see, and then leaned close enough that Marcus could smell cigarettes and mints.

"You are not having a good night, Marcus."

It wasn't a question. Marcus stared at the ceiling. Water dripped from his hair into his eyes. The cinder block with the Michigan stain was still there. Everything was the same. Everything had changed.

"I don't—" His voice was destroyed. A whisper scraped raw. "I don't know anything."

The man straightened. Marcus heard him exhale through his nose, a small, patient sound.

"We have time," he said.

And the cloth came back.

The first pour was warm.

That detail, somehow, was the worst part at the beginning. He'd expected cold—some Hollywood deluge of ice water. But it was warm, body temperature, and that made it wrong, made it feel like it was already inside him. The water moved across the cloth in a slow cascade, saturating the weave, and for one suspended half-second he could still breathe through the damp fabric the way you breathe through a wet snorkel—difficult but possible, air finding its way through the wet threads.

Then the cloth sucked inward.

It sealed against his nostrils. It sealed against the gap of his lips. The water had weight now, pooled in the cloth's weave, and gravity pulled it down, and the fabric pulled tight over his face like something hungry, like the cloth itself wanted to get inside him.

His diaphragm seized.

It wasn't a choice. His body, that stupid animal beneath his mind, understood what was happening before his conscious thought caught up. His chest hitched. His mouth opened involuntarily behind the cloth and tried to pull in whatever it could—

And he pulled water.

Not air. Water. It went over his tongue and down his throat and his body said wrong wrong wrong and every muscle from his pelvis to his collarbone clamped in a single convulsive spasm that was somehow both a gag and a cough and a scream all at once. He arched against the table. His wrists jerked against the zip ties and the plastic cut into the meat of his bones and he didn't care, he needed air, he needed to sit up, he needed—

They stopped pouring.

The cloth still clung to his face. He could hear himself making sounds—wet, hacking, broken sounds, not words, nothing resembling words—through whatever remained of his lungs. His body heaved against the table in violent rhythmic jerks, each one smaller than the last, and each one pulling at the water in his sinuses and his throat so that he was coughing and choking simultaneously, the cloth making everything worse because it wouldn't let his mouth open wide enough to get the water out.

Then someone peeled the cloth away.

Air hit his face.

It was the most beautiful thing he'd ever felt. Nothing. Just oxygen. Moving across his wet skin, rushing into his mouth when he gasped, and he sucked it in so hard his ribs ached, pulling air like he was surfacing from the bottom of a well.

He was shaking. His whole body was vibrating at some frequency beyond his control, and his eyes were streaming, and there was water—warm water, their water—running out of his nose and pooling in the hollow of his throat.

"Where was the radio relay at Kandahar Field?"

The voice was calm. Conversational. The accent was almost gone, smoothed by some university somewhere, and that meant this person had chosen this, had studied and practiced and now spoke to Marcus the way a doctor explains a diagnosis.

Marcus tried to say "I don't know." He didn't know. He was a signals analyst, not field intelligence, and the positions they wanted had been rotated weeks ago anyway. But his voice wasn't working. What came out was a series of wet, rattling syllables that might have been "I don't—" or might have been nothing.

The cloth went back on.

"Please—" His voice was clearer this time. "Please, I don't have—"

Warm water.

The second time was worse because he knew what was coming. His body knew. Before the water even reached his face, his chest locked up, and that was its own kind of drowning—his diaphragm spasming against itself, pulling at closed airways, the mechanical effort of breathing producing nothing, his lungs burning and cramping with carbon dioxide he couldn't expel. The water hit the cloth and sealed it down and the world became this: the taste of wet cotton, the pressure of something flooding his nasal passages, the impossible sensation of being immersed while lying on a table in a room with fluorescent lights and linoleum floors.

He was drowning. He was on his back on a table and he was drowning, and there was nothing he could do about it, and the terror of it was so total that it erased everything else—his training, his name, the fact that there were people who loved him somewhere beyond this room. There was only the water and the cloth and his body's absolute, primal certainty that it was dying.

The sound of his own choking was enormous in his head. He could feel it in his teeth, in his sinuses, in the spaces behind his eyes. His chest heaved and heaved and each spasm pulled in more water and pushed out nothing, and the pressure in his lungs built like a fist closing, and somewhere in the animal depths of his brainstem, in the part of him that was fish and amphibian and a million years of evolution, he felt his body begin to give up.

That was the part no one told you about. Not really. His diaphragm was exhausted. The spasms were slowing. Not because he was getting air—he wasn't—but because his body was running out of fight, was preparing to do the thing it did at the bottom of every deep lake and every ocean: let go. His muscles went slack. The panic, which had been a fire, became something else—something cold and wide and very quiet, and in that quiet he understood that he could die right here, exactly like this, with warm water and a dirty cloth, and it would feel like falling asleep—

They pulled the cloth off.

He came back screaming. Or trying to scream. What actually happened was a violent, wet, full-body convulsion that expelled a mouthful of water across the table and onto the floor, followed by gasping that sounded, to his own ears, like a dog that had been hit by a car. He sucked air in gulping, shuddering pulls, and each breath was agony, and each breath was everything, and he was alive, he was alive, and he hated himself for the gratitude he felt because he was grateful to the people who were doing this to him for stopping.

He was crying. He didn't know when that had started.

The room smelled like old sweat and mildew and something chemical underneath. The fluorescent light buzzed. The man with the educated accent said something in Arabic to someone Marcus couldn't see, and then leaned close enough that Marcus could smell cigarettes and mints.

"You are not having a good night, Marcus."

It wasn't a question. Marcus stared at the ceiling. Water dripped from his hair into his eyes. The cinder block with the Michigan stain was still there. Everything was the same. Everything had changed.

"I don't—" His voice was destroyed. A whisper scraped raw. "I don't know anything."

The man straightened. Marcus heard him exhale through his nose, a small, patient sound.

"We have time," he said.

And the cloth came back.

# The Glitch

The rain came down in sheets on New Meridian's lower district, turning the neon signage into watercolor streaks on Kael Maren's visor. He wiped it clean with the back of his glove and checked the tracker again.

Thirty meters. Directly below.

He crouched on the rooftop edge and studied the building. A decommissioned water treatment plant — all rusted pipes and concrete bones. Perfect place to hide. Terrible place to run from.

The target was named Sorin Voss. Former data architect for Helion Industries. Stole proprietary neural mapping algorithms and tried to sell them on the black market to a rival consortium. Helion wanted him back — or at least wanted their data back. The bounty was 280,000 credits, which was enough to make Kael cross three star systems in a ship held together with stubbornness and epoxy.

Kael dropped to a maintenance ledge, then through an access hatch that groaned in protest. Inside, the air tasted like copper and standing water. Emergency lighting threw long amber shadows across the catwalk.

He heard footsteps — quick, deliberate — echo from somewhere below.

"Sorin Voss," Kael called, his voice steady. "I'm not here to hurt you. I'm here to bring you in. You can make this easy."

Silence. Then a laugh, thin and ragged.

"You're the fourth hunter they've sent," Voss's voice bounced off the walls. "The other three didn't make it back."

"I read the file. They were amateurs."

Kael descended a spiral staircase, each step ringing against the metal. His hand rested on the Mjolnir — a compact directed-energy stun device shaped like a matte black pistol, designed to incapacitate without killing. At least, that was the manufacturer's promise.

Movement. Left.

Voss burst from behind a support column with a length of rebar swung in a wide arc. Kael ducked — felt the wind pass over his skull — and stumbled backward. Voss was taller than expected, lean and desperate, his eyes wide with the particular terror of a man who knows exactly what prison means.

"I'm not going back," Voss snarled, swinging again.

Kael sidestepped, drew the Mjolnir, and fired.

---

The bolt struck Voss center mass.

What happened next unfolded in three distinct phases, each governed by the brutal logic of electricity meeting biology.

**Phase one: Disruption.** The Mjolnir discharged a concentrated beam of high-voltage, low-amperage current — approximately 50,000 volts at less than 4 milliamps. The moment the energy made contact with Voss's torso, it overwhelmed the electrochemical signaling of his nervous system. Motor neurons that controlled skeletal muscle fired simultaneously in a massive, involuntary cascade. Every major muscle group contracted at once — not in the coordinated way of intentional movement, but in a violent, indiscriminate clench. His jaw locked. His fingers seized around the rebar so tightly the tendons stood out like cables. His back arched, spine bending at an angle that would have been impossible under voluntary control.

He didn't scream. He couldn't. His diaphragm and intercostal muscles — the muscles that control breathing — were frozen in full contraction. No air moved.

**Phase two: Collapse.** The involuntary spasm lasted less than two seconds, but it robbed Voss of all balance and motor coordination. When the current cycled off, his muscles released in a staggered wave, like a building losing its floors one by one. He dropped first to his knees, then forward onto his hands. The rebar clattered away. His pupils were dilated, unfocused. Saliva pooled at the corner of his mouth. His heart — which had accelerated dangerously during the discharge — now stuttered through an irregular rhythm, the electrical interference momentarily confusing the sinoatrial node that governed its pace.

His skin at the contact point was flushed red, a sunburn-like mark already forming where the beam had entered. A secondary exit mark bloomed on his lower back where the current found its path to ground through the metal catwalk beneath his boots.

**Phase three: Disorientation.** This was the phase Kael counted on. The stun didn't just stop the body — it scrambled the brain's short-term processing. Voss blinked rapidly, trying to reconcile what his senses were telling him. Sounds came muffled and delayed. His spatial awareness fragmented; the floor seemed to tilt beneath him. He tried to speak, but his tongue and jaw were still recovering from the contraction, and the words came out as a slurred moan.

Pain arrived late — a deep, aching soreness in every muscle that had clenched, like the aftermath of a seizure. His hands trembled. He looked up at Kael with an expression stripped of defiance, replaced by pure animal bewilderment.

---

Kael holstered the Mjolnir and crouched in front of Voss.

"It's done," he said quietly. "The worst is over. You'll feel sore for a few hours. Muscle fatigue, maybe a headache. Nothing permanent."

Voss tried to spit at him, but lacked the coordination. It landed weakly on his own chin.

"Same time next job?" Kael muttered, pulling a pair of electromagnetic cuffs from his belt.

He cuffed Voss's wrists and hauled him to his feet. The man's legs shook but held. Kael activated his comm.

"Hunter Alpha to station. Package acquired. Requesting pickup at grid seven-seven. Target is alive, conscious, and very unhappy about it."

The reply crackled back: *"Copy, Hunter Alpha. En route. Payment on delivery."*

Kael guided Voss toward the stairwell, one hand firm on his shoulder. The rain hadn't let up. Through the broken skylights, he could see New Meridian's skyline flickering through the storm — a city of light and electricity, built on the same forces that had just put a man on the ground.

Voss stumbled on a step and winced.

"Easy," Kael said. "One foot in front of the other."

"I won't forget this," Voss rasped.

Kael almost smiled. "They never do."

---

*—Excerpt from "Bounties & Bodies: A Field Operative's Memoir," published 2387, New Meridian Press*

The first sensation was not pain, but silence. A dense, weighted silence that pressed against Eli’s eardrums. His eyelids fluttered, gritty as sandpaper, and the world resolved into a single, ugly cone of light from a bare bulb hanging inches above his face.

He was seated. No, secured. Thick leather straps bound his wrists and ankles to a chair that felt like bolted-down steel. His right arm, however, was free from the elbow down, suspended in the air by a complex harness of pulleys and chains. It hung over a small, industrial table, on which sat a single object: a scalpel, its blade gleaming under the light, positioned with ceremonial precision.

A whirring click came from a speaker above.

*“Good morning, Eli.”* The voice was calm, detached, like a professor beginning a lecture. *“You have spent forty-seven years building a life of careful, calculated self-preservation. You measure your food, you avoid conflict, you’ve never broken a bone. Your body is your temple, and its integrity is your god.”*

Eli’s breath hitched. His eyes darted around the dim space—concrete walls, riveted steel. A digital clock on the far wall began to count down from 10:00.

*“Today,”* the voice continued, *“your temple requires a sacrifice. To unlock the chair, the mechanism requires a specific biological trigger: the severing of the distal phalanx of your left pinky finger. The knife is provided. The tourniquet is pre-applied.”*

He glanced down. A thick rubber band was indeed cinched painfully tight around the base of his little finger, already making it throb and turn a dusky purple.

The psychological battle began not with fear, but with a surreal, intellectual denial. *This isn’t real. This is a nightmare.* He pulled against the straps, the leather groaning in protest. The chair didn’t budge. The pulley system holding his right arm whined softly, allowing only the slightest movement—a few inches of vertical play, just enough to reach the scalpel.

The clock ticked. 09:47… 09:46…

Panic, cold and sharp, finally lanced through the disbelief. His heart hammered against his ribs, a frantic drumbeat in the tomb-like silence. He began to shake, a full-body tremor that made the chains rattle. His gaze fixed on the scalpel. The light caught a microscopic scratch on its otherwise flawless surface. *Who used it before?*

The conflict was a war fought in the space between his brainstem and his prefrontal cortex. The primal scream of *NEVER HARM THE SELF* clashing with the cold, screaming logic of *OR DIE HERE*. He imagined the act. He felt the shocking cold of the metal, then the inevitable, alien pain. He saw the blood. He felt the lifetime of pristine physical integrity he had so carefully curated shatter in one grotesque moment.

*“Your body is your god,”* the voice echoed in his mind. What was a temple without an altar? What was a god that demanded nothing?

09:12…

He focused on his left hand. The finger was tingling now, numb from the tourniquet. That was a small mercy. He flexed it, watching the movement. It seemed absurdly small, insignificant. *A distal phalanx.* The nail, the whorl of his fingerprint. The thing that had helped him thread needles, feel the texture of silk, press elevator buttons. To sever it was to edit his own history, to rewrite his physical autobiography with a single, bloody stroke.

The preparation was a ritual of grim focus. He had to calm his body. He forced his breathing to slow—in through the nose, out through the mouth. The shuddering lessened. He had to time it. One clean motion. Hesitation would be worse. He imagined the biomechanics: a firm grip, a decisive pull or push—would it be a sawing motion? He banished the thought. *Decisive.*

He looked at his right hand, the one that would wield the blade. It was shaking again. He stared at it, willing it steady. *You are a surgeon,* he told himself. *This is a procedure.* He dissociated, seeing the hand as a separate tool, the finger as a flawed component. The cold logic began to overtake the primal horror. It was arithmetic. Nine functioning fingers and a life, or ten fingers and a slow death in this steel coffin.

08:03…

The choice ceased to be a choice. It was a grim, mechanical necessity. The last vestiges of resistance didn’t vanish; they were drowned out by a wave of pure, survivalist adrenaline. The world narrowed to three points: the clock, the scalpel, the finger.

# The Reckoning

The creak of rope against wood was the only sound on the *Merciless Tide*, save for the low moan of wind through torn sails. Forty men and women lined the port railing, their faces carved from salt and sun, their eyes hard and unreadable. Not one of them looked away.

Captain Edris Thorne stood at the quarterdeck with her arms folded, her long coat bleached pale by years of open sky. Her voice carried without effort.

"Jonas Hale."

The mutineer flinched at his own name. Two crew members shoved him forward across the deck — barefoot, wrists bound, his jaw trembling despite every visible attempt to set it. He stumbled on a coil of rope and nearly fell. Nobody reached out to steady him.

"You stood before this crew and called for my neck," Thorne said, descending the stairs one deliberate step at a time. "You said I'd grown soft. Said I'd lost my nerve." She stopped close enough that he could smell the gunpowder on her gloves. "So now you'll show us all how the brave die."

She gestured toward the plank.

It jutted from the port side like a broken finger — a length of pine, warped and silver-gray, extending eight feet over open water. The sea below was the color of old bruises, deep and sunless even at midday. From the deck, the surface looked deceptively still.

But the water was not empty.

Three shapes circled beneath the hull, dark and deliberate, their dorsal fins cutting the surface in slow, overlapping arcs. Tiger sharks — the long ones, the patient ones. A fourth hung deeper, a shadow among shadows, visible only when it turned and caught a fractured beam of light along its flank. Every now and then a tail broke the surface and slapped the water with a sound like a wet gunshot.

Jonas saw them. His breath changed.

"No," he whispered. Then louder: "Captain — Edris — please."

"You had your say yesterday." Thorne's expression didn't shift. "Now the sea has its say."

The first mate, a gaunt woman named Maret, stepped forward and cut the rope binding Jonas's wrists. She didn't meet his eyes. "Walk," she said quietly. "Don't make them drag you."

Jonas stood at the base of the plank, his toes curled over the edge of the deck, staring at the narrow board beneath him. The wind pushed his lank hair across his face. His hands opened and closed at his sides, grasping at nothing.

He took one step. The plank groaned.

Below, the circling shapes quickened. One of the sharks rolled — a flash of pale belly, a black eye glinting upward, as if it could feel the vibration of footsteps through the water.

Two steps. Three. The board bent under his weight and the crew heard a sound come out of him — not a scream, not a sob, but something in between, something that came from the hollow place where courage had been.

Four steps. He was halfway out now, suspended between the ship and the open Atlantic, the plank no wider than his foot. The sharks had drawn closer to the surface, their movements no longer patient. They'd begun to bump the underside of the plank — he felt it, a dull impact through the wood, and he froze, his arms pinwheeling.

He looked back. Every face behind him was stone.

"God," he said to no one, or to all of them, or to the indifferent sky.

Five steps. Six. The plank dipped. Salt spray misted his shins.

Seven steps. He was at the end. The wood shuddered beneath him, slick with spray. Below, the largest shark turned on its side and opened its mouth — rows of teeth, serrated and overlapping, catching the light like broken glass.

Jonas Hale stood there for a long moment, swaying, the horizon tilted and mad around him.

He did not jump.

The plank gave a final, exhausted crack, and he fell.

The splash was enormous. The water frothed white, then red. The sharks converged in a fury of thrashing tails and dark, rolling bodies. The sound that reached the crew was brief and terrible and then it was gone, and the sea smoothed itself back to its patient, glimmering calm.

Captain Thorne watched for a count of ten. Then she turned to face her crew.

"Let that be the last mutiny on my ship," she said. "The sea remembers. So do I."

She climbed back to the quarterdeck, and the *Merciless Tide* sailed on.

# The Weight of Seconds

The vest came to life before Marcus understood what he was wearing.

He'd felt the weight first — not heavy, exactly, but *wrong*. A dull, distributed pressure across his chest and ribs, like a wet sandbag someone had buckled against him while he slept. Then the cold. The adhesive backing of the duct tape had sealed itself to his undershirt, and through the cotton he could feel the dense, rectangular shapes — three of them, maybe four — sitting just above his diaphragm. They were warm now, leaching heat from his body like stones pulled from a fire.

His fingers found the wires.

They were thin — thinner than he expected — insulated in red and blue and white, crossing and recrossing his sternum in a tangled nest. The copper inside was stiff but yielding, like the stem of a dried flower. He followed one with his thumb, tracing it from a taped junction box near his left pectoral down to a module pressed against his solar plexus. The tape securing it was electrical tape, wound in overlapping layers, and its rubbery texture caught against the rough of his fingerprint.

The ticking was small.

Not a clock ticking. Something faster, more electric — a relay clicking in and out of itself, somewhere inside the junction box. He pressed his ear against his own chest and heard it multiply, that mechanical insect heartbeat, and realized the frequency matched the blinking of a red LED he could just see through the seam of his shirt. *Tick-tick-tick-tick.* Each cycle was maybe a third of a second. Each one was gone before he could count it.

His breathing changed.

It was shallow now, up high in his throat, the kind of breathing that doesn't feed the brain. He could feel sweat starting along the back of his neck, cool and then immediately hot, and his palms had gone slick — so slick that when he tried to grip a blue wire near the collarbone, his fingers slid off the insulation and the wire sprang back against his skin with a faint *snap*.

"Don't," he said to himself, but the word came out wrong, pitched too high, the vowel stretched thin like a wire itself.

He looked down. The duct tape was gray, industrial, puckered where it lapped over the edges of the blocks. He could see hand-written notation in black marker on one of the charges — a serial number, or maybe a timer readout. The numbers meant nothing. Everything meant nothing except the ticking, which had not stopped, which would not stop, which was the only thing in the room that had any certainty left.

His fingers hovered over the junction box again.

The wires were warm now too. All of them.

# The Hallway

The bedroom door stuck. It always stuck. Marcus should have fixed it months ago, and now—pushing against it at 2:47 in the morning with a bladder screaming for relief—the warped wood felt like a personal betrayal.

It gave with a groan.

He stood in the hallway, blinking against the dark. The house was his house, same as it had been for six years, but the darkness made it a stranger. The hallway stretched ahead of him, longer than it had any right to be at this hour, the bathroom door a pale rectangle at the far end.

He took a step. The floorboard beneath him—a loose one he'd been meaning to fix, there were so many things he'd been meaning to fix—let out a low, deliberate creak.

From the living room to his left, something shifted.

Not a sound, exactly. More like the suggestion of a sound. The way air moves when a door opens slowly, or when a person adjusts their weight on carpet.

Marcus stopped.

He stood perfectly still in the hallway, bare feet on cold hardwood, and listened. The refrigerator hummed. The house settled with its usual chorus of ticks and groans. A car passed somewhere distant, its headlights briefly painting a moving stripe across the ceiling.

Nothing. He was being ridiculous.

He took another step.

Behind him—in the bedroom he'd just left, the bedroom he was now realizing had been slightly too warm when he woke up, the window cracked open wider than he'd left it—a floorboard answered his.

Not the loose one. A different one. The one by the closet.

Marcus turned around slowly. The bedroom door was still open, a black mouth breathing cool air into the hallway. He could see nothing past the threshold, but the darkness felt occupied the way an empty room with a closed closet door feels occupied.

"Hello?" he said, and hated how thin his voice sounded. Hated even more how it felt wrong to say anything at all, like he'd just announced exactly where he was standing.

Silence.

Then, from the bedroom, the slow exhale of a mattress releasing weight.

His phone was on the nightstand. Twelve feet behind him. His keys, his wallet, the baseball bat he kept meaning to move from the closet to the bedroom—all of it back there. He thought about the kitchen, the knives, the lock on the front door. He thought about the window above the sink that was always painted shut.

The knife drawer in the kitchen would make noise. He'd have to open it, and the runners squeaked. They always squeaked.

From the bedroom doorway, a shadow shifted. Not a figure—something more subtle than that. The quality of the darkness changed, thickened, and for half a second Marcus could have sworn the air itself leaned toward him.

He backed up one step. Then another. The loose floorboard screamed beneath him.

The shadow came forward.

Not fast. Not yet. Just enough to confirm what the darkness had been telling him for the past ninety seconds—that the bedroom was not empty, that the warmth he'd woken to was not the heater, that the window was open for a reason.

Marcus ran.

He didn't decide to run. His body decided before his mind caught up, and by the time his thoughts arrived he was already past the bathroom door, already reaching for the kitchen light switch, already turning—

The light came on, and the kitchen was empty.

He stood there, chest heaving, eyes raking every corner. Counter. Table. Window above the sink, shut tight. Knife block on the counter—six handles, all accounted for. The back door, deadbolted.

Safe. He was safe.

Then he noticed the wet footprints on the tile floor.

They came from the living room. They led to the counter. And they stopped at the knife block.

One knife was missing from the block.

Behind him, the hallway light that he'd left on went out.

---

Marcus didn't turn around. Couldn't. His hand found the largest knife left in the block—his hand was shaking, the handle was shaking, he was shaking—and he held it out behind him, a prayer more than a weapon.

The only sound was his own breathing and, from the hallway, the softest whisper of a shoe on hardwood.

Coming closer.

Not fast. Not yet. Just enough to confirm what the darkness had been telling him for the past ninety seconds—that the bedroom was not empty, that the warmth he'd woken to was not the heater, that the window was open for a reason.

Marcus ran.

He didn't decide to run. His body decided before his mind caught up, and by the time his thoughts arrived he was already past the bathroom door, already reaching for the kitchen light switch, already turning—

The light came on, and the kitchen was empty.

He stood there, chest heaving, eyes raking every corner. Counter. Table. Window above the sink, shut tight. Knife block on the counter—six handles, all accounted for. The back door, deadbolted.

They came from the living room. They led to the counter. And they stopped at the knife block.

One knife was missing from the block.

Behind him, the hallway light that he'd left on went out.

Coming closer.

# The Trench

The first sign is a taste — metallic, acrid, like biting through a copper wire. You don't yet understand what you're breathing, but your body does. The involuntary flinch arrives before cognition: a sharp inhale through the nose, then the cough that begins at the diaphragm and hammers upward.

The gas settles low, pooling in the trench like dirty water. It follows the earth's gravity. You feel it first in the deepest branches of your lungs — not the throat, not the mouth, but somewhere behind the sternum where the bronchioles narrow into the alveolar sacs. Those tiny air sacs, each thinner than a soap bubble, begin to weep. The membranes flood. You are drowning in your own tissue.

---

**The respiratory collapse follows a rhythm:**

Stage one is denial. You cough hard, once, twice, expecting to clear it. The air doesn't come back right. There's a wet resistance now — a crackling, like crumpling cellophane inside your chest. Every inhale requires conscious effort. Your intercostal muscles, the thin bands between your ribs, work desperately to expand a cage that no longer cooperates.

Stage two is panic wrapped in a strange, dissociative calm. The oxygen debt builds. Your lips take on a blue-grey cast as hemoglobin struggles to find air to bind. You gasp — open-mouthed, head tilted, neck taut — pulling hard through fluid instead of atmosphere. Each breath is shallow, each one less effective than the last. The diaphragm spasms. Your abdomen clenches in waves. You can feel the fluid now, heavy and warm, pooling at the base of the lungs. You cannot lie down. If you lie down, you drown faster.

Stage three is the body's final argument. The coughing becomes constant, ragged, uncontrollable — productive now, bringing up a frothy, pink-tinged sputum that smells of burned metal. Your chest heaves with the effort of a marathon runner, but you've gone two steps in a trench that smells like bleach and almond and death. The world narrows to the single mechanical task of pulling air in and pushing it out. Vision tunnels. The sound of your own breathing becomes the loudest thing in the world.

---

**The mind fractures differently.**

There is the soldier who knows he is dying, and there is the animal that refuses to accept it. They speak at the same time. The soldier calculates — *how long since exposure, how far to the aid station, who is nearby.* The animal simply screams through the body: flailing, clawing at the collar, ripping open the tunic to give the lungs more room they cannot use.

Time distorts. Seconds feel geological. Between gasps, there is a strange lucidity — a hyper-awareness of small details. The texture of the trench wall. The way a rat watches you from a dark corner. The sound of boots on duckboards, running *away* from you. You understand, with terrible clarity, that you are now a hazard. The men you shared rations with this morning cannot touch you without dying the same death.

There is rage in that. And beneath the rage, a loneliness so total it becomes physical — as if the gas has dissolved not just your lung tissue but every connection you had to another human being.

---

**If you survive** — and many did, though survival meant months of convalescence and permanent scarring of the lungs — you carry the memory like a foreign object lodged in the chest. Not just the fear, but the *taste*. That copper-metallic sharpness. For years afterward, any strong chemical smell — bleach, cleaning fluid, a struck match — would send your hands shaking and your diaphragm into spasm, your body relearning a lesson your mind could not forget:

*The air itself can be a weapon. The most basic act of being alive — breathing — can be turned against you.*

# The Cold Kindness

The restaurant had closed an hour ago. Vinnie, the last waiter, had locked the front door, set the alarm, and driven home to his wife in Yonkers. Now the only light came from the kitchen's fluorescent hum and a single candle on the corner table, where Salvatore Marino sat with his hands folded over a linen napkin.

The man across from him — Marco — kept adjusting his tie. He'd been adjusting it for ten minutes.

"You remember my father, Marco?"

Marco stopped touching his tie. "Of course, Mr. Marino."

"When someone disappointed my father, he would pour them a glass of wine. Good wine. He'd sit with them, look them in the eye, and say, *'I hope you find peace.'*" Salvatore let the candlelight shift between them. "Then he'd leave the bottle."

Marco's jaw tightened. "I don't — I'm not sure I understand."

"You understand."

A long silence. Somewhere outside, a truck downshifted on the avenue.

"Mr. Marino, whatever you've heard — I can explain. DiAngelo is making noise to save himself. He's—"

"Marco." Salvatore's voice didn't rise. It softened, which was worse. "I didn't ask you here to argue a case. There's no case. There's just... *the arrangement.*"

Marco exhaled through his nose. His hands were flat on the table now, palms down, like a man pressing against glass.

"My sister has kids," he said quietly.

"I know. Three. Good kids. I hear the oldest plays soccer."

"Then you know why I—"

"I also know you went to DiAngelo's people. I know you gave them the shipment schedule for Newark. I know you did it for sixty thousand dollars and a promise they'd keep you safe." Salvatore tilted his head. "Sixty thousand. That's what I'm worth to you, apparently."

Marco didn't speak.

"Here's what's going to happen." Salvatore folded his napkin once, precisely, and set it beside his glass. "You're going to retire. Quietly. No one hears from you again. You settle your affairs this week — call your sister, visit your mother, do whatever makes you feel right with God."

"And if I don't?"

Salvatore looked at him with something that almost resembled pity. "Marco. You already have."

He raised a hand. From the kitchen doorway, two men stepped into the light — unhurried, silent, the way people move when the work has already been decided.

Salvatore stood. He buttoned his coat.

"Finish the wine," he said, without looking back. "It's a good vintage."

---

The front door opened and closed. The street was quiet. The candle burned between the three men who remained, and the bottle sat half-full on the white tablecloth, catching the light like something sacred.
